content.text:
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
[Non-English content] Good afternoon everyone and welcome to TSMC's Q3 2022 Earnings Conference Call. This is Jeff Su, TSMC's Director of Investor Relations and your host for today. TSMC is hosting our earnings conference call via live audio webcast through the company's website at www.tsmc.com, where you can also download the earnings release materials. If you are joining us through the conference call, your dial-in lines are in listen-only mode. The format for today's event will be as follows. First, TSMC's Vice President and CFO Mr. Wendell Huang will summarize our operations in Q3 2022, followed by our guidance for Q4 2022.
Afterwards, Mr. Huang and TSMC CEO Dr. C.C. Wei will jointly provide the company's key messages. We will open the line for Q&A. As usual, I would like to remind everybody that today's discussions may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to significant risks and uncertainties, which could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in the forward-looking statements. Please refer to the safe harbor notice that appears in our press release. Now I would like to turn the call over to TSMC CFO, Mr. Wendell Huang, for the summary of operations and the current quarter guidance.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Thank you, Jeff. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us today. My presentation will start with financial highlights for Q3 2022. After that, I will provide the guidance for Q4. Q3 revenue increased 14.8% sequentially in NT dollar, or 11.4% in US dollars as our Q3 business was supported by strong demand for our industry-leading 5nm technology. Q3 gross margin increased 1.3 percentage points sequentially to 60.4%, slightly ahead of our guidance as we enjoyed a more favorable foreign exchange rate and cost improvement efforts. Total operating expenses accounted for 9.8% of net revenue as compared to 10% in the previous quarter. Operating margin increased 1.5 percentage points sequentially to 50.6%, mainly due to better operating leverage.
Overall, our Q3 EPS was TWD 10.83, and ROE was 42.9%. Now let's move on to revenue by technology. 5nm process technology contributed 28% of wafer revenue in the Q3, while 7nm accounted for 26%. Advanced technologies, which are defined as 7nm and below, accounted for 54% of wafer revenue. Moving on to revenue contribution by platform. Smartphone increased 25% quarter over quarter to account for 41% of our Q3 revenue. HPC increased 4% to account for 39%. IoT increased 33% to account for 10%. Automotive increased 15% to account for 5%. DCE decreased 2% to account for 2%. Moving on to the balance sheet. We ended the Q3 with cash and marketable securities of TWD 1.5 trillion.
On the liability side, current liabilities decreased by TWD 38 billion, mainly due to the decrease of TWD 116 billion in short-term loans, partially offset by the increase of TWD 70 billion in accrued liabilities and others. Long-term interest-bearing debt increased by TWD 88 billion, mainly as we raised TWD 60 billion of corporate bonds during the quarter. On financial ratios, accounts receivable turnover days decreased one day to 36 days. Inventory days decreased five days to 90 days, primarily due to higher wafer shipment during the quarter. Now, let me make a few comments on cash flow and CapEx. During the Q3, we generated about TWD 430 billion in cash from operations, spent TWD 266 billion in CapEx, distributed TWD 71 billion in Q4 2021 cash dividends and raised TWD 60 billion from corporate bond issuances.
Overall, our cash balance increased by TWD 43 billion to TWD 1.3 trillion at the end of the quarter. In US dollar terms, our Q3 capital expenditures total $8.75 billion. I have finished my financial summary. Now let's turn to our current quarter guidance. Based on the current business outlook, we expect our Q4 revenue to be between $19.9 billion and $20.7 billion, which represents a 0.4% sequential increase at the midpoint. Based on the exchange rate assumption of one US dollar to TWD 31.5 , gross margin is expected to be between 59.5% and 61.5%. Operating margin between 49% and 51%. This concludes my financial presentation. Now, let me turn to our key messages.
I will start by making some comments on our Q3 and Q4 profitability. Compared to Q2, our Q3 gross margin increased by 130 basis points sequentially to 60.4%, mainly due to a more favorable foreign exchange rate and cost improvement efforts despite continued inflationary cost pressures. Compared to our Q3 guidance, our actual gross margin exceeded the high end of the range provided three months ago as our guidance was based on exchange rate assumption of one US dollar to TWD 29.7. Whereas the actual Q3 exchange rate was $1 to TWD 30.32. This created about 80 basis point difference in our actual Q3 gross margin versus our original guidance.
We have just guided our Q4 gross margin to be flattish sequentially to 60.5% at the midpoint. A more favorable exchange rate assumption will be offset by a lower capacity utilization rate. As a reminder, 6 factors determine TSMC's profitability: leadership, technology development, and ramp-up, pricing, cost reduction, capacity utilization, technology mix, and foreign exchange rate. Looking ahead to 2023, we face challenges from N3 ramp dilution, higher year-over-year increase in depreciation cost, rising inflationary costs, semiconductor cyclicality, and overseas fab expansions. To manage our profitability in 2023, we are working closely with our customers to support their growth and continue to strategically and consistently sell our value. We are also working diligently on our internal cost improvement.
Excluding the impact of foreign exchange rate, of which we have no control over, and taking the other five factors into consideration, we believe a long-term gross margin of 53% and higher is achievable. Next, let me talk about our 2022 CapEx. As I have stated before, every year, our CapEx is spent in anticipation of the growth that will follow in future years. Three months ago, we set our 2022 CapEx would be closer to the lower end of our $40 to 44 billion range. Now, we are further tightening up this year's capital spending and expect our 2022 CapEx to be around $36 billion. About half of the change is due to capacity optimization based on the current medium-term outlook, and the other half is due to continued tool delivery challenges.
Out of the around $36 billion CapEx for 2022, between 70% to 80% of the capital budget will be allocated for advanced process technologies. About 10% will be spent for advanced packaging and mask making, and 10% to 20% will be spent for specialty technologies. Looking ahead, we will continue to manage our business prudently given the near-term uncertainties, and adjust and tighten up our capital spending where appropriate. That said, our commitment to support customers' growth remains unchanged, and our disciplined CapEx and capacity planning remains based on the long-term structural market demand profile. We will continue to work closely with our customers to plan our long-term capacity and invest in leading-edge and specialty technologies to support their growth while delivering profitable growth to our shareholders. Now, let me turn the microphone over to C.C.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Good afternoon, everyone. First, let me start with TSMC's more resilient near-term demand outlook. We concluded our Q3 with revenue of TWD 613.1 billion or $20.2 billion, supported by strong demand for our industry-leading 5nm technologies. Moving into Q4 2022, we expect our business to be flattish as customers' ongoing inventory adjustment is balanced by continued ramp-up of our 5nm technologies, supported by smartphone and HPC applications. We expect our full-year gross in 2022 to be mid-30% in US dollar terms. On the demand side, we continue to observe softness in consumer end-market segment. Other end-market segments such as data center and automotive-related remain steady for now for TSMC, but we start to see the possibility of adjustment down the road. On the inventory side, our customers and the supply chain continue to take action to adjust their inventory.
We expect the semiconductor supply chain inventory to peak in Q3 this year and start to reduce in Q4 this year. We also expect it will take a few quarters through H1 2023 to rebalance to a healthier level. While the ongoing inventory correction will also affect TSMC, we expect our business to be less volatile and more resilient than the overall semiconductor industry during this period, supported by three key factors that are TSMC's cost base in the foundry industry. First, our technology leadership and depreciation is much stronger today as compared to previous years. This enable TSMC to win business and enables our customer to win business in their end markets despite the semiconductor cyclicality.
Secondly, through our comprehensive design ecosystem and optimized process technologies, we are able to address and capture the structural increase in demand for computation and build a strong portfolio in high performance computing. Third, our strategic relationship with our customers are long-term in nature, and we continue to work closely with our customer on technology development, capacity planning, and pricing to support their long-term demand and growth. As a result, we continue to see strong demand for our leading node, except the N7, and steady demand for our differentiated specialty technologies and mature node. Looking ahead to 2023, with the successful ramp-up of N5, N4P, N4X, and the upcoming ramp of N3, we will continue to expand our customer product portfolio and increase our addressable market.
Thus, while the ongoing semiconductor inventory correction will affect our H1 2023 utilization rate, we expect our business to be supported by stronger demand for our differentiated and leading advanced and specialty technologies, and for 2023 to be a growth year for TSMC. Next, let me talk about the N7, N6 demand outlook. Due to end market weakness in smartphone, PCs, and customers product schedule delay, starting Q4 this year, our N7, N6 capacity utilization will not be as high as it has been in the past three years. We expect this to persist for a few quarters through H1 2023 as the semiconductor supply chain inventory takes a few quarters to rebalance to a healthier level, and we have adjusted our N7, N6 CapEx accordingly.
We believe the N7, N6 demand is more a cyclical issue rather than structural, and expect our N7, N6 demand to pick up in H2 2023. Longer term, we continue to work closely with our customers to develop specialty and differentiated technology, and are confident to drive additional wave of structural demand to backfill our N7, N6 capacity over the next several years. Thus, our 7nm family will continue to be a large and long-lasting node for TSMC. Now, I will talk about our N3 and N3E status. Our N3 is on track for volume production later this quarter with good yield. We expect a smooth ramp in 2023, driven by both HPC and smartphone applications. Our customers' demand for N3 exceeds our ability to supply, partially due to the ongoing tool delivery issues.
We expect N3 to be fully utilized in 2023. We expect N3 revenue in 2023 to be higher than N5 revenue in its first year in 2020, and for N3 to contribute mid-single digit percentage of our wafer revenue in 2023, as our overall revenue base is much larger today than in 2020. N3 will further extend our N3 family with enhanced performance, power, and yield, and offer complete platform support for both smartphone and HPC applications. N3E development is progressing ahead of plan, and volume production is now scheduled for H2 2023. Despite the ongoing inventory correction, we observe a high level of customer engagement at both N3 and N3E, with a number of tape-outs more than 2x than that of N5 in its first and second year.
Thus, we are working closely with our tool supplier to address the tool delivery challenges and prepare more 3nm capacity to support our customers' strong demand in 2023, 2024, and beyond. Our 3nm technology will be the most advanced semiconductor technology in both PPA and transistor technology when it is introduced. We are confident that the N3 family will be another large and long-lasting node for TSMC. Finally, let me talk about the future driver of leading node adoption. TSMC's mission is to be the trusted technology and capacity provider for the global logical IC industry for years to come. Our job is to help our customers unleash their innovations and enable them to capture greater value and win in their end markets.
As the industry continues to pursue scaling, it is true that geometry shrink is slowing down and becoming more challenging for everyone due to rising process complexity. However, it is also true that demand for energy efficient computing is accelerating in an intelligent and connected world as technology is becoming more pervasive and essential in people's lives. Thus, the semiconductor industry value in the supply chain is increasing, and the value of technology platform is expanding beyond the scope of geometry shrink alone and increasingly toward greater power efficiency. As a result, our customers value much more than simply transistor cost. System performance and power efficiency has become key motivation for customers to adopt our leading-node technologies.
By working closely with our customer on technology development, our N3 and N2 will deliver full node strides in performance and power benefits while offering the industry's most advanced transistor scaling. We expect strong demand for our leading-node technologies, driven by both smartphone and HPC applications to fuel our long-term revenue growth of 15% to 20% CAGR over the next several years in US dollar terms. With our leadership in both leading-edge process technology and 3D solutions, TSMC's technology cadence remains constant to deliver the value of our technology platform. We will continue to extend our overall competitiveness and technology leadership while delivering a predictable technology cadence that helps our customers to enhance their product competitiveness and grow their markets well into the future. This concludes our key message, and thank you for your attention.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, C.C. This concludes our prepared statements. Before we begin the Q&A session, I would like to remind everybody to please limit your questions to two at a time to allow all the participants an opportunity to ask questions. Should you wish to raise your question in Chinese, I will translate it to English before our management answers your question. For those of you on the call, if you would like to ask a question, please press the zero, then one on your telephone keypad now. If at any time you would like to remove yourself from the questioning queue, please press zero two. Now, let's begin the Q&A session. Operator, can we please proceed with the first participant on the line?
Operator
Yes, Jeff. The first one to ask a question, Gokul Hariharan from JPMorgan. Go ahead, please.
Gokul Hariharan
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Yeah, good afternoon, and thanks for taking my question. Congrats on the great results, especially in the margins. So first question is on N7 and N6, this utilization slack that we are observing. Could we give a little bit more detail on why that is happening and why we think this is a short-lived couple of quarters issue and we get a pickup in the utilization in H2? I think last time we saw this was for 20nm, but that was. That lasted for much longer period of time. So could you also give us some kind of comparison with what happened back in 20nm and why this is going to be very different?
Maybe a little bit more color on what are the areas of backfill demand for N7 and N6 as the high-end smartphone processors and HPC start to move on to N5 and then N3. That's my first question.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Gokul, please allow me to summarize your first question. Gokul's first question is on N7, N6. He wants to understand what is driving the utilization slack, why we believe it is short-lived and that the demand for N7, N6 can pick up in H2. Then also on the little bit longer term outlook, why we believe that N7 can be backfilled, and it will not be like N28 a few years ago with a few years of underutilization.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, Gokul, let me answer your question first on the why demand drop. Demand drop because of market become soft, as we said in the weakness in the smartphones and PCs. A big factor is our customers' product schedule delay. All in all, put all together, we think that our utilization has been affected in Q1 this year and all the way to H1 2023. For the longer term, we continue to work closely with our customer. Actually, let me also say that this is a cyclical issue. It will pick up anyway, and we believe it will pick up in H2 2023.
For the longer term, we continue to work closely with our customer to develop specialty and differentiated technology to drive additional wave of structural demand from consumer, RF, connectivity, et cetera, and other applications to backfill our N7, N6 capacity, and so for the next several years. That's all I can say.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Does that answer your first question, Gokul?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Gokul?
Gokul Hariharan
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Yeah, I'm here. Sorry.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay.
Gokul Hariharan
Managing Director, JPMorgan
My second question would be on the CapEx outlook. Now that we bring down the CapEx slightly for 2022, could you talk a little bit about what is the outlook direction for 2023 at least, if not absolute numbers, but just direction? Are we going to be flattish or it's likely to be going down? Second is also, could you also give us an update on the schedule for the new fabs, Kaohsiung, Kumamoto, Nanjing, and Arizona? Is there any change in the schedules in terms of these fabs coming into production? Thank you.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay. Thank you, Gokul. Gokul's second question is on CapEx and capacity. First he wants to hear, of course, he says that we have tightened up our CapEx in 2022. He is asking for 2023 directionally, is there an indication of 2023 CapEx? And then he would also like an update on our expansion plans in Kaohsiung, Nanjing, Arizona, and Kumamoto.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay, Gokul, let me answer you the first part. For 2023 CapEx, it is too early to comment. We will provide you with a specific guidance in January. However, as we said, we have tightened up our 2022 CapEx to reflect the current medium outlook as well as tool delivery issues. Looking ahead to 2023, we will continue to be careful and manage our business prudently given the near-term uncertainties. We will adjust and tighten up our capital spending where appropriate. We will continue to work closely with our customers to invest for the long-term structural market demand profile to support their growth.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, let me answer the second part of Gokul's question. Gokul, you ask about the progress of our Arizona fab, Nanjing fab, and Kaohsiung. Let me say that Arizona fab will continue and on schedule. There's no doubt about it because this is a N5 family. We still have a very strong demand. For Nanjing, we just get our one-year authorization for 28nm expansion, so it is on schedule also. For Kaohsiung, initially we planned two fabs at the beginning of a 28nm expansion and the N7. Now, N7 has been adjusted and so. But 28nm expansion is continuous and on schedule.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Also Kumamoto.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Oh, okay. Also, the Japan fab is on schedule to meet the customers' demand. Okay, Gokul?
Gokul Hariharan
Managing Director, JPMorgan
Got it. Thank you very much.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
All right. Thank you, Gokul. Operator, can we move on to the next participant, please?
Operator
The next one to ask questions is Bruce from Goldman Sachs. Go ahead, please.
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Thank you for taking my question. My first question is regarding to the HPC, which is a key growth driver for TSMC for the coming years. However, with the recent US new restriction to China, what do you think about the HPC demand moving forward? What kind of impact? Is it going to see a slowdown from China, or are we gonna see the acceleration from the non-China side?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Bruce's first question is on HPC. He notes HPC, we have said repeatedly will be TSMC's key growth driver and main engine the next few years. He wants to know, I believe, Bruce, the impact of the recent US regulations, does that affect the overall HPC demand or the overall profile? Is that correct?
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Yes. What's the impact from this new restriction to TSMC and overall industry?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay, let me answer that. Bruce, it's based on our initial reading and feedback from our customers. The new regulation set the control threshold at very high-end specification, which is primarily used for AI or supercomputing applications. Therefore, our initial assessment is the impact to TSMC is limited and manageable. We are continuing to closely monitor the situation to ensure that we are all in full compliance with all the rules and regulations. For the longer term, it's too early to really assess all the true impact or influence, but we will give you the update in the following earnings call.
Okay.
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Okay. Understand that. Thank you. My next question is regarding to the cyclical nature for the 7nm. We also noticed that most of your other nodes, you know, the capacity utilization rate is still at a very, very high level or at least much better than 7nm as management mentioned. Why is 7nm so cyclical? Because, you know, maybe because you guys are too big that you have to keep new industry or what is the difference between your 7nm and your other nodes?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Bruce Lu's second question is looking at N7 specifically. He wants to know, you know, our other nodes' utilization still seems to be holding up well. Why specifically N7 is more cyclical and utilization is, you know, not as high as it has been. Is that correct, Bruce?
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Yes.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
It just happened, you know, that most of my smartphone and PCs, the customer are using N7, N6 node. You know, it just happened. The market weakness in the smartphone and PC happened at the same time. Also other customers or product schedule delay. All in all, that's why it become lower utilization rate as compared with other node. If you want to compare with the N5 or you compare with the 28nm, all those are very, you know, still a very high demand. We continue to enjoy the higher market share.
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
I want to dig in a bit because we get used to like, you know, TSMC will manage your customers' product and the overall outlook, even with some paperwork that you can figure it out with someone else. You know, anything different with this time that 7nm you cannot have as good as, you know, your other node.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Bruce wants to still understand, you know, why the 7nm utilization cannot be as high as the other nodes if, you know, we work closely with customers and it's well planned.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, again, Bruce, we work closely with our customer, but our customer get caught in this inventory correction and the market downturn. They didn't know this one, probably two quarter before. You know, at the beginning of this year, they are still give us a very high number of their forecast. You know, it just happened. As we said, we believe this is a cyclical issue, and it will pick up. Before that, it probably will take a few quarters.
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
I understand. Thank you. We just get too used to it to expect TSMC always deliver a much better result.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
I understand.
Bruce Lu
Research Analyst, Goldman Sachs
Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Thank you, Bruce. Operator, can we move on to the next caller, please?
Operator
Next, we have Randy Abrams from Credit Suisse.
Randy Abrams
Managing Director and Head of Semiconductor Research, Credit Suisse
Yes. Okay. Thanks for taking my question. Yeah. I wanted to ask a two-part first question. You mentioned in the prepared remarks about HPC and auto continue to be stable, but it seemed the signal may change. If you could give your view how you see inventory levels and some of the forward demand outlook from those areas. The second part, just wanna see if we could get a bit better visibility on H1. Q1, how do you see it versus normal signal? And then for the trough, do you expect Q1 could be the bottom, or do you see the trend that we could be towards Q2?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Randy's question is really looking at, again, from the end demand segment data center, and automotive, we say are remaining steady at TSMC for now. He wants to understand, though, what is the outlook down the road and what does that mean for inventory levels. Secondly is also he wants to see if we can provide some more granularity about Q1 outlook versus seasonality, and whether we think Q1 can be the bottom for the industry. Is that correct, Randy?
Randy Abrams
Managing Director and Head of Semiconductor Research, Credit Suisse
Yeah, that's correct.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay. Let me answer this one. Of course, we say that, so far our customer give us their demand forecast. The data center and automotive related are still steady. Now the market becomes soft, and we are taking more conservative way in our planning for 2023. That's why we say that, we don't rule out the possibility there might have some correction also. You know, we did not see it right now, to be frank with you. For the inventory correction in the 2023, all we want to say is like that, we expect probably 2023, the semiconductor industry will likely to decline. TSMC also is not immune.
We believe our technology position, strong portfolio in HPC, and longer term strategic relationship with customer will enable our business to be more resilient than the overall semiconductor industry. That's why we say in 2023 is still a growth year for TSMC, and the overall industry will probably decline.
Randy Abrams
Managing Director and Head of Semiconductor Research, Credit Suisse
Okay. Again, I'll ask a quick follow-up and then the second question. I guess just the sense, because it's still very firm in Q4, if you're seeing a pretty meaningful falloff into Q1, like some years 10%, 2019 declined over 20%. Just try to get a rough feel of the type of decline factor you're gaining some content and share. That's the follow-up to the first. The second question, actually just on gross margin because of a lot of headwinds, I think, Wendell, you talked about. If you could give just on a couple of these, differentiation factoring the recent CapEx, how much up, and whether it's also front-end or more back-half loaded, given the 3nm ramp.
For the startup cost for N3, if you expect similar to N5, given smaller percent of revenue, how much dilution from N3? Okay. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay, Randy. Let me summarize. Randy, quick, I think we will not comment on the Q1, but I think we can make some comment just sort of in terms of the overall inventory picture, in the, you know, looking into next year.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, actually, if you ask my opinion on the inventory picture and the inventory correction, it's too early to provide a specific number. However, the inventory correction will likely see its biggest impact sometimes in H1 2023.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. The second part related to the gross margin, maybe Wendell can address what is the outlook for differentiation next year? Is it front- or back-end-loaded? Also, what type of dilution we expect from 3nm as it ramps in 2023.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay, Randy. For full year differentiation for next year, it's too early to talk about that. This year is mid-single digit increase year-on-year. Next year, we expect it will likely to be meaningfully higher. We will give you the guidance in January. As to the dilution from N3, it will be between 2 to 3 percentage point, from the whole year basis, on our gross margins.
Randy Abrams
Managing Director and Head of Semiconductor Research, Credit Suisse
Okay. Actually, one follow-up. Do you think on a single quarter with the inventory correction, do you expect to keep the 53 and above, factoring we're coming from a very high level, even through that H1 inventory correction?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Right. It is too early to talk about 2023 gross margin including a quarter over quarter. Even with all these cost challenges, we believe our structural profitability can be maintained, and we are confident to deliver a long-term gross margin of 53% and higher. Okay?
Randy Abrams
Managing Director and Head of Semiconductor Research, Credit Suisse
Okay. Great. Thanks for all the help.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, Randy. Operator, can we move on to the next participant, please?
Operator
Next one to ask questions, Charlie Chan from Morgan Stanley.
Charlie Chan
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
Hi. Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. My first question to management is about whether the company consider a share buyback, because as a company seems to suggest a recent inventory correction is just a cyclical, you're still very positive on long term. I think the share price really reveal company's long-term value, right? Also, shareholders value. I'm not sure if a company want to do share buyback or cash returns.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Charlie's first question is that, you know, although there's cyclicality, the long-term outlook appears good. Would the company consider doing a share buyback?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Yeah, Charlie, we constantly review all the different options of returning cash to shareholders. For share buyback at this moment, we are not considering it. We think our cash on hand will be better kept to invest in our capital expenditure to make a better return for our shareholders.
Charlie Chan
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
Okay. Understood. Thank you. Also my second question is also about the US sanction impact. I know the company said that impact is limited and the long-term impact remains to be seen, right? My question is about the China market to TSMC. Is that as strategic as before after this event?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Charlie's second question, he wants to know with the recent US regulations and the impact, how do we see the China market? Is it still a strategic market for TSMC? Is that correct, Charlie?
Charlie Chan
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
Yeah. How does the company think about TSMC's kind of long-term picture? How important is China going forward?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Charlie, I would like to say that every region is important to TSMC. However, let me say that under the condition of what complies with all the rules and regulations, TSMC will continue to serve all the customer all over the world. That's our position.
Charlie Chan
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
Okay. Including China.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
All the customers.
Charlie Chan
Managing Director, Morgan Stanley
Okay. Okay. Got it. Thank you. Those are my questions. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, Charlie. Operator, can we move on to the next participant, please?
Operator
Next one to ask question is Sunny Lin from UBS.
Sunny Lin
Research Analyst, UBS
Hi. Thank you for taking my questions. Congrats on the steady performance. My first question is on the geopolitical tensions. I wonder, given some of the considerations regarding the geopolitical issues, how would you evaluate the longer term impact from customers potentially diversifying from Asian foundries, and how are you managing the risk? Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Sunny's first question is that, given the geopolitical tensions, you know, how do we evaluate the long-term impact and the risk of customers using other foundries? Is that correct, Sunny?
Sunny Lin
Research Analyst, UBS
That's right. Thank you.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay. Sunny, we still believe the most important thing is the technology leadership in manufacturing and our customer trust. In different location, manufacturing or whatever, still, we still think that technology leadership is the most important thing. That's our strategy. We make it simple, that technology, manufacturing and customer trust.
Sunny Lin
Research Analyst, UBS
Got it. A quick follow-up, is that going forward, should we assume an acceleration of your overseas expansions, just to diversify the production sites, i.e., if there could be a fab built in Europe?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Sunny's second question, Can she assume that we will continue to increase the overseas global footprint expansion and also particularly in Europe?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, we will continue to increase our overseas portion in manufacturing based on customers' need, in fact, based on the business opportunity and also based on the operations efficiency and economics. Whether we are going to be in the Europe, we are in preliminary evaluation and do not rule out any possibility. Again, I would like to say the decision were based on customers' need, business opportunities, operation efficiency, and cost economics.
Sunny Lin
Research Analyst, UBS
Got it. Thank you. I actually have a second question, on HPC. With the increasing usage of chiplets, how would you manage the risk, in the case that some dies are made at the other foundries and that have production issues and therefore impacting the production at TSMC as well? Thank you very much.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Sunny's second question is with increasing usage and adoption of chiplets in HPC, how would we manage the risk in case, I think, Sunny, you're saying if dies at other companies or places have production issues, would the... How would, you know, how do we manage the risk of that impacting TSMC?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, Sunny-
Sunny Lin
Research Analyst, UBS
That's right. Thank you.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Sunny, in fact, we would like our customer manufacturing every chip inside TSMC for sure. If there's a case that they have to use other companies or dies, we will work with our customer closely and minimize all the risk that as time goes by. That's what we are doing right now.
Sunny Lin
Research Analyst, UBS
Got it. Thank you. That's very helpful. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, Sunny. Operator, can we move on to the next participant, please?
Operator
Right now we have Laura Chen from Citi.
Laura Chen
Head of Citi Research, Citi
Hello. Hi. Thank you for taking my question. I appreciate that if you can share with your latest plan in your Nanjing fab. Like as C.C. already mentioned, you got the license for the 28nm in Nanjing. I'm just wondering that, do you also need the license for the 16nm in the Nanjing fab? And also, going forward, what's your plans of your operation in China? That's my first question. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Laura's first question is about Nanjing fab and our plans. She notes that we have received the one-year authorization, so our 28nm expansion continues as planned. Her question is, do we also need a license for the 16nm that we have in Nanjing? And then also, what is our long-term future expansion plans in China?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Sunny, let me answer the first part.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Laura.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Sorry. It's Laura. Let me answer the first part.
Laura Chen
Head of Citi Research, Citi
Yeah.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
The one-year authorization that we received covers the Nanjing facility, so it's both the 28 and 16.
Laura Chen
Head of Citi Research, Citi
Okay, great. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
The second part is, what is our long-term expansion plans for China?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay. As C.C. said, we will be operating, serving all the customer under the condition that we will fully follow and in compliance with all the rules and regulations.
Laura Chen
Head of Citi Research, Citi
Okay. That's very clear. My second question is also about the fab globally, in the longer term. We know that, in overseas operation, usually they will have a much higher, operational cost. How would that impact the TSMC's long-term margin trend, or in our view? Or maybe you can give us some estimation about your estimate of the percentage of the margin in different region or the cost difference comparing to Taiwan.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Laura's second question is around our expansion of our global manufacturing footprint. She notes she wants to know that overseas fabs are the costs higher? Do we have a breakdown how much the cost difference is in Japan and US versus Taiwan? Overall, with overseas expansion and if they are higher costs, how does this impact our long-term profitability and margin?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay. Laura-
Laura Chen
Head of Citi Research, Citi
Thank you. Yeah.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Let me answer this question. The initial costs of overseas fabs are indeed higher than TSMC's fabs in Taiwan, and it's mainly because of higher labor costs in different layers of the supply chain. We continue to work closely with the US government as well as with our customers and supply chain partner to manage and minimize the cost gap. Now, through these efforts, we believe we can continue to earn the proper return and deliver the long-term gross margin of 53% or higher.
Laura Chen
Head of Citi Research, Citi
Okay, that's very clear. Thank you very much.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, Laura. Operator, can we move on to the next participant, please?
Operator
Next one to ask questions is Rolf Bulk from New Street Research.
Rolf Bulk
Senior Equity Research Analyst, New Street Research
Thank you for taking my question. I was hoping you could give some more context around the 3nm tool shortages that you mentioned. Is that primarily lithography and then, specifically EUV related? Or do you also see shortages in other tool segments? Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Rolf's first question is around 3nm and the tool shortages. He wants to know if this is very just specific to lithography tools and EUV specifically, or is it more, I guess, broad based?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Let me answer the question. Actually, it's more broad-based because our demand is high, and certainly the photolithography tools are included, and one of the most important ones.
Rolf Bulk
Senior Equity Research Analyst, New Street Research
Thank you. That's very useful. Then as my follow-up question, it would be great to get an update on your N2 nodes. With your current visibility, is the node still on track timing-wise? And is there anything you can share on how you think about yields of N2 versus N5 and N3 at the same stage of development?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Rolf's second question is on N2. He would like an update. Are we still on track? What is the timing for N2? And also if there's an update on yields as compared to N3 and N5 at similar stage.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay. I said before N2 is a very difficult one, but you know, our progress so far so good. Actually, it's a little bit ahead. We are going to have a mass production introduced in 2025. Our customers' engagement so far are very, let me say that, comparable with the N3, N5. The status today is very comparable to the N5 and also N3. We are happy to see that, you know, our progress so far.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Does that answer your question, Rolf?
Rolf Bulk
Senior Equity Research Analyst, New Street Research
Great. Thank you very much.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Yeah. Thank you, Rolf. Okay, operator, let's move on to the next participant, please.
Operator
Next one we have Charles Shi from Needham & Company.
Charles Shi
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Needham & Company
Good afternoon. Thank you for taking my questions. I have two, both on CapEx. The first question is really. I understand you are not here to guide 2023 CapEx, but I think a few years ago, you did provide some long-term CapEx, a range of CapEx, when your long-term CAGR guidance was 5% to 10%. You think $10 to 12 billion CapEx is gonna support that long-term CAGR. I think you just reiterated your long-term CAGR to be 15% to 20%. Do you kinda have a similar range of CapEx for us to think about over long term? Again, I'm not asking you about 2023 CapEx here.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Charles' first question is about really I think, Charles, you're asking about CapEx correlation with growth. He notes that in the past we, you know, had said our long-term growth would be 5% to 10%. During that period, we said we would spend between TWD 10 to 12 billion. Without asking about 2023 specifically, Charles wants to know, now we believe we will grow between 15% to 20% CAGR, in the next few years, what type of CapEx range does that imply or should he assume? Is that correct, Charles?
Charles Shi
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Needham & Company
Yeah. Correct.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay, Charles. Let me try to answer this question from the capital intensity point of view. When we invest heavily to capture the future growth, the capital intensity will be high, like last year and this year.
If the growth slows down, the capital intensity may become lower. Now longer term wise, we think that a normal or a reasonable capital intensity may be somewhere between mid- to high 30%, longer term wise.
Charles Shi
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Needham & Company
Thank you. The second question is about very near term into the next quarter, basically. Because you just slashed your 2022 CapEx, I mean, from what you guided one quarter ago by about $4 billion. If I hear correctly, half of that can be attributed to the tool delivery issues. But the other half, can you clarify a little bit? Because you kind of said it's about capacity optimization. Is that kind of like a $2 billion reduction in CapEx mostly a reduction of the equipment spending or is it something else you're reducing here and trying to improve the capital or capacity optimization here? Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Charles' second question is on the CapEx, and he is asking, we have now guided to around TWD 36 billion versus, you know, close to TWD 40 billion last time. We have said half of it is related to tool delivery, and the other half is capacity optimization for the midterm demand outlook. His question is, with the capacity optimization, is this mainly also reduction in tools or is this some other issue? Is that correct, Charles?
Charles Shi
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Needham & Company
Yes. Correct. Thank you.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay. Charles, I think you're right that the half of that difference comes on tool delivery issue. The other half is the capacity optimization. By that, and that's because of the current uncertainty in market conditions, so we're tightening up our capital budget. It relates to the whole capacity. It's including tools, including the other stuff within the CapEx. Yeah. It's mainly N7.
Charles Shi
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Needham & Company
Thank you very much.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Yeah. I think.
Charles Shi
Managing Director and Senior Analyst, Needham & Company
Got it. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Yeah. It's tools, and also as C.C. and Wendell mentioned, some of the adjustments we have made to our N7, N6 capacity and CapEx, due to the aforementioned reasons. Thanks. Okay. Thank you, Charles. Operator, can we move on to the next participant?
Operator
Next one we have Brad Lin from BofA Securities. Go ahead, please.
Brad Lin
Director, BofA Securities
Thank you very much for taking my question. First of all, still, congratulations on the strong earnings. My first question is about, well, if we look at the long pages of the new regulations from the US on China, it can be really broad and, of course, with a key aim on the supercomputing. However, given the wide variety and also wider application of chips that TSMC makes, isn't it, in theory, difficult to identify and make sure the chips and the business complying with the regulation? Will there be some extra cost and overhead cost by that which we should notice in the future? Thank you. That's my first question.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Brad's first question is with the new US regulations. He knows it's very long and very wide in scope. He is wondering if it's very hard to interpret, and therefore, will this result in greater overhead cost for TSMC to ensure that we are and continue to be fully compliant with all the regulations?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, actually, although it looks about more than 100 pages, but from our initial reading and feedback from our customer, actually the regulation is very simple to be understood, like a control threshold at a very high-end specification. For example, like a 600 Gb/s, you know, the bandwidth or those kind of things. Or it's very easy to be understood, and we continue to work with our customer to make sure that we fully comply with the regulation.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Brad would also like to know, Wendell, from a financial standpoint, will we incur more overhead costs, as a result?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
At this moment, we don't think so.
Brad Lin
Director, BofA Securities
I see. Thank you very much. Just a slight follow-up, because the regulation is just aiming at the supercomputing, but I know in a supercomputer, definitely there are some still some low-end chips used inside. If we happen to make those and then we are not sure that it is going there, when we produce them, will that cause some confusion or bring some trouble to us? Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Brad's second question is, you know, in a supercomputer, there may be very specific high-end restrictions, but there's also, you know, companion chips, other chips used. Would that cause us an issue?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
The companion chip, yes and no. No restriction or no regulation at all. We rely on our customer to work with their own customer for that kind of a product.
Brad Lin
Director, BofA Securities
Got it. Thank you very much. Maybe if I may, second question would be, clearly, many countries would like to build their own foundry or build their own domestic supply chain. We have learned that the cost will be a major downside. My question would be, can we charge different pricing that's basically demanded by our clients, right? With higher costs, if they want to buy from US or buy from Europe, can we charge a higher pricing if that's based on specific node? If we think about the bright side, would you please share how TSMC could well utilize this kind of opportunity to strengthen our competitiveness in the long run? Thank you. That'll be my all questions.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Brad, second question is about, you know, he notes that many countries would like to have domestic semiconductor manufacturing. TSMC, we are, as C.C. said, also increasing and expanding our global manufacturing footprint. With higher cost, will we be able to charge a higher price? I guess that is essentially his question.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Actually, TSMC's pricing is strategic and consistent. All I can say is we will continue to share our value. The values come from the technology manufacturing and also that our, you know, relationship with our customers. Whether it is in a different country or it's in a different place, it's not in our consideration. Again, I would like to say we are continuing to share our value, and our pricing is strategic.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Thank you.
Brad Lin
Director, BofA Securities
Thank you very much.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, Brad. Operator, can we move on to the next participant, please?
Operator
Next one we have Mehdi Hosseini from Susquehanna International. Go ahead, please.
Mehdi Hosseini
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Susquehanna International Group
Yes, sir. Thanks for taking my question. I also have my first multi-part question. I'm just looking at your customers' inventories. And days of inventory are at a 25-year high. It seems, based on your commentary, that the demand forecast, especially looking at H1, has weakened. It seems to me that the inventory correction is going to sustain to Q2, and most likely, your shipment would be declining sequentially in Q1 and Q2. Just looking at your customers' inventory, is that a realistic view of H1? Because you also highlighted the fact that inventory correction is going to sustain throughout H1. I'm not asking for a guide. I'm just trying to better reconcile your customers' inventory with your comment. I have a follow-up.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Mehdi's first question is on inventory. He notes customers' inventory levels are very high. We have talked about our observation from an industry level that demand is softening in, you know, consumer segments. His question is what is the outlook and, you know, do we expect the inventory correction, I guess, to be more notable as we go into H1 2023? Is that correct, Mehdi?
Mehdi Hosseini
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Susquehanna International Group
Yes. Particularly, you've always had your wafer shipment up in Q2, but I think 2023 could be an exception, and it could probably decline. That's how I frame my question. The question is, could wafer shipment decline in Q2 for the first time in many, many years?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Well, Mehdi, our current forecast, actually, our supply chain inventory were peaking Q3 this year. We observed that the inventory will start to reduce in Q4 this year. We expect you will see its biggest impact in the H1, actually, H1 2023. The detail of Q1, Q2, or something like that, we are not ready to share with you yet, because, you know, we continue to work with our customer and to understand that their demand.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
And with-
Mehdi Hosseini
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Susquehanna International Group
If I may have just a quick follow-up to that. Does that imply that your customer forecasts are changing so rapidly that we have to wait for January calls to get the final read on the H1?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
No, Mehdi, I think we have always, in the past, we will guide for 2023 and talk about 2023 outlook and Q1, during the January conference, right? But I think C.C. has already said-
Mehdi Hosseini
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Susquehanna International Group
Okay.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
That with the inventory correction, we expect our business to be more resilient during both the downturn and upturn, given our technology leadership, and that 2023 is a growth year for TSMC. Okay? We will not comment further on-
Mehdi Hosseini
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Susquehanna International Group
Got it.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Q1 or Q2.
Mehdi Hosseini
Senior Equity Research Analyst, Susquehanna International Group
Okay. My second question, it has to do with differentiation that was down.
In Q3, down year over year and Q over Q. This is despite the fact that CapEx was up 65% in 2021. Does that have anything to do with tool optimization? To that extent, as a second part of the question, would you consider converting 7nm tool to 5nm and 3nm?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Mehdi, second question first is differentiation. Why, you know, it is down Q-on-Q and year-on-year. And then also would we consider converting capacity.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Okay. Mehdi, differentiation, we look at it from a whole year point of view. For this year, as I mentioned, we expect it to be up year on year by mid-single digits. For next year, it will be meaningfully higher, but we will share with you more in January. Please understand that every year, there are differentiation newly going into the differentiation table, and also there are differentiation coming off of the differentiation table. What you're looking at is the net result. As to converting N7 capacity to N5, as we mentioned earlier, N7 demand issue is cyclical rather than structural. At this moment, I don't think we have that kind of plan.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Thank you, Mehdi. In the interest of time, operator, maybe we can take the last questions from the last two participants, please.
Operator
Yes, sir. Next one to ask question, Patrick Chen from CLSA. Go ahead, please.
Patrick Chen
Head of Research, CLSA
Thank you for taking my question. You talked about 2023 to be still a growth year. Would you say that growth is pretty much the same compared to what you expected a quarter ago, or it is lower? If so, what's driving this lower growth expectation?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Patrick's first question is about 2023. Is the growth that we see for 2023, how does it compare versus our expectation for three months ago for 2023? And what is driving this?
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Yeah, well, I think it's too early to talk more, too much about 2023. We maintain our statement that 2023, we still expect it as a growth year. Okay.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Do you have a second question, Patrick?
Patrick Chen
Head of Research, CLSA
Okay. That's helpful. Maybe a follow-up, if I may, any leading indicators that you are monitoring that could, you know, help you or help us determine the growth outlook aside from, you know, monitoring the client's wafer orders?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Patrick Chen's second question is looking with inventory correction. He wants to know if there's any leading indicators that we can look at or he should look at to see when, you know, indication that the cycle is bottoming.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
That's very hard to answer your question. Actually, you know, if you look at the whole industry, from the smartphone and PCs, and you read all the quarterly report from all major player, you can sense that when it will go up and when it's a downturn. We definitely have some information. Internally, we do the analysis. Today we are taking a very conservative way for our planning. That's all I can share with you.
Patrick Chen
Head of Research, CLSA
Thank you. I guess that's what we've been doing as well. Obviously we don't have a crystal ball. Well, I don't have any further questions. Thank you for taking my question. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Thank you. Operator, can we take the last participant, please?
Operator
Yes. The last one to ask question is Frank Lee from HSBC. Go ahead, please.
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
All right. Thank you. I wanted to ask, I guess the question on your N3, N3E. Is the ramp for both nodes gonna be around the same time, or is there gonna be some difference in scheduling?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Frank's first question is on ramp for N3 versus N3E. Is it at the same time?
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
Yes.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Yeah. Okay.
Actually, it's not at the same time. Right now we are ramping up by N3, and N3E supposed to be one year apart, but because of the progress so well, so we might pull in a little bit for two or three months. That's all. They are still not at the same time.
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
Right. Okay. My second question is, you know, I know you've reiterated your margin, long-term gross margin target being unchanged. I guess given the headwinds you're seeing now, through H1 next year, you know, with the currency move already gone up quite a bit, utilization rates dropping, is this... Are you gonna see any potential change in the pricing strategy? I know it can't come too specifically, but, you know, you have seen some price increases in the last 12 months or so. From going forward, though, would the pricing strategy still be relatively unchanged given the change in the overall market environment?
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Okay. Frank's second question is related to pricing, with the inventory correction, and with some of the cost challenges. He wants to know, will there be any changes to our pricing strategy during this correction? Is that correct, Frank?
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
Yes. Yeah, thanks.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay, Frank, let me answer the question. Again, I want to stress that our pricing actually is strategic and consistent. You say that, do we have any plan to change it? No, it will be consistent. All right. You know, not based on any cycle or opportunistic, and we actually most important, we always work closely with our customer to provide our value and to help them to win their own end markets.
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
Right. No, I'm not suggesting there's any optimistic pricing, but just given the market situation has changed for your clients who are probably going through a more difficult time, would there be some change in strategy to help align with them as well? Or would they largely still be the same policy that we've seen?
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
We stay the same. We are consistent.
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
Okay.
C.C. Wei
CEO, TSMC
Okay?
Frank Lee
Managing Director and Head of Asia Technology Research, HSBC
Okay. Thank you.
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Thank you, Frank. All right. This concludes our Q&A session. Before we conclude today's conference, please be advised that the replay of the conference will be accessible within one hour from now. The transcript will become available 24 hours from now, both of which will be available through TSMC's website at www.tsmc.com. Thank you for joining us today, and we hope you will join us again next quarter. Goodbye, and have a good day.

content.text:
Jeff Su
Director of Investor Relations, TSMC
Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to TSMC's Q1 2022 earnings conference call. This is Jeff Su, TSMC's Director of Investor Relations and your host for today. To prevent the spread of COVID-19, TSMC is hosting our earnings conference call via live audio webcast through the company's website at www.tsmc.com, where you can also download the earnings release materials. If you are joining us through the conference call, your dial-in lines are in listen-only mode.
Operator
The format for today's event will be as follows: First, TSMC's Vice President and CFO, Mr. Wendell Huang, will summarize our operations in Q1 2022, followed by our guidance for Q2 2022. Afterwards, Mr. Huang and TSMC's CEO, Dr. C.C. Wei, will join me to provide the company's key messages. Then we will open the line for Q&A. As usual, I would like to remind everybody that today's discussions may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to significant risks and uncertainties, which could cause actual results to differ materially from those contained in the forward-looking statements. Please refer to the Safe Harbor notice that appears on our press release. Now, I would like to turn the call over to TSMC's CFO, Mr. Wendell Huang, for the summary of operations and the current quarter guidance.
Wendell Huang
VP and CFO, TSMC
Thank you, Jeff. Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. My presentation will start with financial highlights for Q1 2022. After that, I will provide the guidance for Q2. Q1 revenue increased 12.1% sequentially in TWD terms, or 11.6% in US dollar terms. Our Q1 business was supported by strong HPC and automotive-related demand. Q1 gross margin increased 2.9 percentage points sequentially to 55.6%, mainly as we continue to sell our value and improve cost. Operating margin increased 3.9 percentage points sequentially to 45.6%, primarily due to lower vaccine donation expense as compared to Q4. Overall, our Q1 EPS was TWD 7.82 and ROE was 36.2%.
Now, let's move on to revenue by technology. 5nm process technology contributed 20% of wafer revenue in Q1, while 7nm accounted for 30%. Advanced technologies, which are defined as 7nm and below, accounted for 50% of wafer revenue. Now, moving on to revenue contribution by platform. All six platforms increased in Q1. Smartphone increased 1% quarter over quarter to account for 40% of our Q1 revenue. HPC increased 26% to account for 41%. IoT increased 5% to account for 8%. Automotive increased 26% to account for 5%. DCE increased 8% to account for 3%.
Moving on to balance sheet. We ended Q1 with cash and marketable securities of TWD 1.3 trillion. On the liability side, current liabilities increased by TWD 83 billion, mainly due to the increase of TWD 63 billion in accrued liabilities and others, and the increase of TWD 30 billion in short-term loans, partially offset by the decrease of TWD 21 billion in accounts payable. Long-term interest bearing debt increased by TWD 19 billion as we raised TWD 20 billion of corporate bonds during the quarter. On financial ratios, accounts receivable turnover days decreased two days to 38 days, while days of inventory remained at 88 days.
Now let me make a few comments on cash flow and CapEx. During the Q1, we generated about TWD 372 billion in cash from operations, spent TWD 262 billion in CapEx, and distributed TWD 71 billion for Q2 2021 cash dividend.
